_meta.interpretation: Yes, clearly. Comparing each customer with themselves, revenue rose on average by roughly a quarter of the earlier level (the test's mean_diff against avg_revenue_before, the average spend before, in the data row); the interval for that rise is narrow and well above zero, and the effect size is large. Pairing is what makes this sharp: each customer is their own baseline, so the wide differences between customers drop out. The test says spending rose, not why: the test period mixes the treatment with a gradual drift over time, so the rise belongs to both.
_meta.question: Did customers spend more during the test period than they did before it?
_meta.description: Paired t-test of revenue against revenue_before, row by row: the average before-to-after change per customer, which mixes the treatment lift with the time drift. AGG_AVERAGE of revenue_before gives the baseline the change is read against.
_meta.name: paired_t_before_after
